Chapter 7: New Horizons—Learning, Sharing, and the World Beyond.
With the windmill spinning steadily, something amazing starts to happen. Doors that once felt tightly shut are now swinging open. News of the boy’s invention travels far beyond his village. Visitors, teachers, even the occasional journalist—they all carry his story with them, turning it into something bigger than he ever imagined.
Letters start arriving from distant towns. Some are written in careful English, others in the warm, familiar tones of Chichewa. Each letter feels like a new connection—proof that the world is much wider, and maybe even more welcoming, than he ever thought possible.
Then, the invitations begin. A local school asks him to come and speak to their students. And at first? He hesitates. What could he possibly say that matters?
But when he stands in front of all those eager faces, he remembers what it was like to be hungry for knowledge—to spend hours in the library, chasing the thrill of discovery. So, he tells his story honestly. He talks about the doubts, the setbacks, and those small, stubborn victories that kept him going. The students listen closely. Some nod, understanding exactly what he means. Others jot down notes, their eyes shining with big dreams of their own.
One day, a teacher from a nearby town reaches out and offers to help him apply for a scholarship. The process feels overwhelming—so many forms, essays to write, interviews that make his heart race. But he faces each step the same way he built his windmill—with patience and determination.
When the acceptance letter finally arrives, it’s like watching the sun rise for a second time. Everything feels brighter, and the path ahead glows with new possibility.
At his new school, the world opens up even more. Science comes alive in ways he never expected—labs filled with equipment, teachers who seem to love questions, classmates who share his curiosity. He dives into new lessons: solar panels, water pumps, and all the ways technology can change lives for the better.
And through it all, he learns something important—knowledge isn’t just for keeping. It’s a gift you’re meant to share.
Back home, his absence is felt, but his presence lingers in the windmill’s steady turning. Letters and visits keep him connected, and whenever he can, he returns—eager to pass on what he’s learned.
The village, once shaped by scarcity, now pulses with quiet hope. Kids dream about building their own inventions. Parents talk about a future where hunger is only a memory, no longer a shadow that follows them.
